### Overall Assessment: Useful with Caveats

Munoz, Shores, Weathers and Woods use the two most recent usable waves of the Civil Rights Data Collection (2017–18 and 2020–21), linked to CCD enrollments and SEDA geography, to put one clean descriptive fact on the record: in U.S. public high schools, Black students attend schools with 1.16 more security-staff FTE per 1,000 students than White students (1.02 in 2020–21) and Hispanic students 0.79 more (0.66 in 2020–21), and the bulk of that gap is non-sworn security guards, not sworn officers — 0.97 of the 1.16 Black–White gap is SSGs and 0.17 is LEOs, while the Hispanic–White gap is SSGs entirely (the LEO gap is 0.026, p = .158, in 2018 and −0.055 in 2021; Table 1, p.7). A Goldhaber-style geographic decomposition then locates the Black–White gap mostly between districts within the same metro area (0.944 of 1.163 in 2018) rather than between schools within districts (0.258), with the Hispanic–White gap split more evenly between metros and districts (0.476 vs. 0.491). Those two results rest on near-universe data and an internally consistent table (all twelve between-region residuals reproduce from the printed components), and they carry the policy point the brief was written for: a district that removes police but keeps guards, as Chicago did, leaves most of the measured staffing disparity in place. That is what the paper should be cited for, and the field can rely on it. The brief should not be cited for its three most quotable interpretive lines. The RQ3 claim that racial segregation is "the strongest and only significant predictor" of metro-level SSG gaps, and the conclusions that guard deployment "operate[s] independently of racial composition or poverty" and that LEO placement "follows entirely different mechanisms" (p.10), rest on a multivariate regression that appears in no exhibit in the article — Figure 2 is bivariate, reports no N of CBSAs, and plots Black/Hispanic enrollment share where the text defines the predictor as the non-White share — and the segregation association is partly built in, since a within-metro exposure gap cannot exist without between-school sorting (the authors call segregation "necessary but not sufficient" on p.6). The regional "paradox" (regions with more students of color staff fewer personnel) is read off an unestimated residual with no standard error (−0.356 for Black–White; Table 1 note) and a four-point figure whose x-axis is described three incompatible ways and whose LEO line in Panel A slopes the opposite direction from the "clear downward slope" the text describes. The "roughly 80% of the gap" attribution is arithmetically right against the net gap but ill-defined as a share, because the positive components sum to 131% of it. The abstract's "disparities are present across all geographic scales and for LEOs" overstates Table 1, where no division-level component approaches significance (p ≥ .73) and the Hispanic–White LEO gap is never positive. And the between-wave comparisons should not be read as trends: 2020–21 was a pandemic year the paper never mentions, the handling of New York City's force-certified 2017–18 staffing data is not stated, and the one component that did change significantly — the Black–White SSG gap falling from 0.974 to 0.823 (p = .035) — goes unmentioned in the prose even though it cuts against the Discussion's speculation that districts are substituting guards for police. Reproducibility is the weakest dimension for a paper built entirely on public data: no code, no software, no data statement, no count of high schools, no standard-error method, an estimating equation that lives only in an unavailable supplement, and SSG and LEO columns that do not add to the total column without explanation. The literature framing also needs one correction before repeating: the claim that prior distributional work "focused exclusively on LEOs" overlooks the SSOCS-based security-measures literature, and E. G. Owens (2017) is cited as correlational evidence that guards may soften the school-to-prison pipeline when it is a quasi-experimental study of sworn police. The right posture is to quote Table 1's first row and its SSG/LEO split in per-1,000 units, cite the between-district concentration qualitatively, and attach caveats to everything downstream of it.

#### Key Strengths

- The SSG/LEO split on universe data is the durable contribution, and it is large: of the 2017–18 Black–White high-school gap of 1.163 security FTE per 1,000 students, 0.974 is guards and 0.172 is sworn officers, and the Hispanic–White gap (0.792) has no positive LEO component at all (Table 1, p.7). Prior CRDC-based descriptions (Lindsay et al., 2018; Gleit, 2022) covered officers only; this is now the reference for "guards, not just police."
- The exposure measure (student-weighted FTE per 1,000, not mere presence) is the right estimand for "who is around more security staff," and the paper explains why prevalence understates intensity in large secondary schools (pp.3–5).
- The geographic decomposition is transparent and internally consistent: every between-region residual in Table 1 reproduces from the other rows to the third decimal, and the qualitative finding that the Black–White gap sits mostly between districts within metros (0.944 vs. 0.258 within districts) survives any reasonable reading of the shares.
- The Black–White versus Hispanic–White contrast is informative in its own right: the Hispanic–White gap is split nearly evenly between metros (0.476) and districts (0.491), suggesting different geographic mechanisms for the two groups (Table 1, p.7; text, p.8).
- The paper is honest about its scope where it counts — it frames itself as "the descriptive component" (p.3), concedes "no rigorous causal evidence" on SSGs (p.2), discloses the residual status of the between-region row (Table 1 note), and names the 2015–16 exclusion and the NYC 2017–18 reporting problem (p.4).

#### Key Concerns

- The RQ3 headline is reported but not shown. "Racial segregation is the strongest and only significant predictor" and the three lettered conclusions (p.10) depend on a multivariate regression with no coefficients, standard errors, N, weights, year, or specification anywhere in the article, and no pointer to a supplemental table (the only supplemental reference in that paragraph is Figure A1, for LEOs). Figure 2 (p.11) is bivariate. The segregation result is also partly mechanical, and "only significant predictor" among three collinear CBSA-level constructs does not license "operates independently of racial composition or poverty."
- The regional "paradox" (pp.8, 10) is built on an unestimated residual (−0.356 Black–White, −0.295 Hispanic–White; no p-value by construction) and on Figure 1, which has N = 4 regions, fits weighted by the x-variable itself, an x-axis that the axis label (within-region percent Black/Hispanic), the note's formula (Black_r/ΣBlack_r) and the text ("share of the national Black ... population," p.8) describe incompatibly — the plotted Panel A values sum to about 0.57, so they are within-region shares — and an LEO line in Panel A that rises with Black share rather than falling.
- Several sentences overrun Table 1. The abstract's "present across all geographic scales and for LEOs" and the text's "gaps remain at every other finer spatial level—division, CBSA, and district" (p.8) are contradicted by division components of 0.014–0.041 with p-values of .73–.97 and by a Hispanic–White LEO gap that is null in 2018 and negative in 2021; "roughly 80%" is a share of a net gap whose positive components sum to 1.519; the Hispanic–White pattern is attributed to "state-level factors" though no state level appears in Table 1; and the between-district component is glossed as "district-level choices about how security staff is allocated across schools" (p.10), which describes the smaller within-district component and treats sorting across districts as a choice.
- The two-wave comparison is under-documented and under-discussed. The paper never mentions COVID-19 although 2020–21 is a pandemic year; it does not say whether NYC's force-certified 2017–18 records (or the ~3% and ~5% of schools missing staffing data) were dropped or imputed; it quotes the change p-value (.001) for the 2021 Hispanic–White LEO gap as if it were the level test; and it never mentions the one significant component change — the Black–White SSG gap fell from 0.974 to 0.823 (p = .035) — which runs against the Discussion's untested substitution story.
- Reproducibility falls short of what all-public data allow: no data or code statement, no software, no N of high schools/districts/CBSAs, no definition of "high school," no merge key or CBSA-assignment rule (including for cross-division CBSAs and non-CBSA schools), no replacement value or grouping for the winsorization, no standard-error or clustering method, an estimating equation that exists only in the unavailable supplement, and SSG + LEO ≠ total in Table 1 (0.974 + 0.172 = 1.146 vs. 1.163) with no explanation.

#### What to Rely On

- The national high-school exposure gaps in the first row of Table 1 (p.7): Black–White 1.163 (2017–18) and 1.021 (2020–21); Hispanic–White 0.792 and 0.656; all significantly different from zero (p < .001). These are enrollment-weighted differences in school-level staffing rates on near-universe public data and should be approximately reproducible by anyone with the files.
- Guards, not sworn officers, account for most of the gap: 0.974 of 1.163 for Black–White in 2018 (0.823 of 1.021 in 2021), and effectively all of the Hispanic–White gap (SSG 0.749 vs. LEO 0.026, p = .158, in 2018; SSG 0.712 vs. LEO −0.055 in 2021). The Black–White LEO gap is real but small (0.172, 0.179).
- For Black–White gaps, the largest single geographic component is between districts within the same metro area (0.944 in 2018, 0.832 in 2021), and the within-district-between-school component is much smaller (0.258, 0.243). Quote the per-1,000 values rather than a percentage share.
- Hispanic–White gaps are distributed more evenly across scales: between-CBSA (0.476) and between-district (0.491) components are of similar size in 2018, and both dwarf the between-school component (0.105).
- The arithmetic policy corollary: removing sworn officers alone leaves most of the measured staffing disparity in place. This follows directly from the SSG/LEO split and says nothing about student outcomes.
- The bivariate, descriptive statement that metro-level Black–White and Hispanic–White SSG gaps rise with SEDA's Theil segregation index and with racial differences in exposure to school poverty, and are flat to slightly declining in minority enrollment share (Figure 2, p.11) — as a pattern, not a mechanism.

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- "Segregation is the strongest and only significant predictor," and conclusions (a)–(c) on p.10 — the multivariate regression is not reported in the article; Figure 2 is bivariate with no N; the segregation association is partly by construction; and the LEO "different mechanisms" claim rests on a non-significant result in an unavailable appendix figure. Ask for the regression table before citing.
- The regional "paradox" that regions with more students of color use less security staff — an unestimated residual with no standard error, illustrated by four points with an inconsistently defined x-axis, and false for LEOs in Panel A (the LEO line slopes upward with Black share; the LEO between-region residual is +0.009).
- "Roughly 80% of the total gap" arises between districts within CBSAs — correct as 0.944/1.163, but the four positive components sum to 131% of the net gap; against the sum of positive components the between-district share is about 62%. The qualitative ranking survives; the percentage does not partition anything.
- "Disparities are present across all geographic scales and for LEOs" (abstract) — division-level components are never significant (p ≥ .73) and the Hispanic–White LEO gap is null (2018) or negative (2021).
- Any 2018→2021 trend, or any inference about the police-free-schools movement — two waves, one of them a pandemic year the paper does not discuss, with NYC's 2017–18 missingness handled in an unstated way. The only significant component change (Black–White SSGs, 0.974 → 0.823, p = .035) is unmentioned, and it points away from, not toward, the suggested substitution of guards for police.
- The p = .001 quoted for the "slightly negative" 2021 Hispanic–White LEO gap (p.8) — that is the change-from-2018 test; the test against zero is reported as .000.
- The effect-size conversions on p.6 ("0.87 times the mean," "0.45 SD," "0.26 SD") — the SSG mean (1.11) and SD (2.15) appear only in prose with no stated basis (school- or student-weighted, which year), the LEO mean and SD are never reported, and a national SSG mean of 1.11 is hard to square with Figure 1's regional SSG means, which run from roughly 0.35 (South) to 1.28 (Northeast).
- "District-level choices" (p.10) as the source of the between-district component — the decomposition cannot separate district allocation decisions from the sorting of students across districts, and the omitted SSOCS literature gives reasons (size, urbanicity, incident rates) to treat allocation as one hypothesis among several.
- The literature framing: "prior studies ... focused exclusively on LEOs" (p.3) is too broad given the SSOCS-based security-measures literature (Nance; Kupchik and colleagues; NCES Indicators); E. G. Owens (2017) is not correlational evidence that guards attenuate the pipeline; Pigott et al. (2018) is cited for arrests though its title concerns expulsions; Mallett (2016) is a critical review, not qualitative evidence on guards. Verify before repeating.
- Robustness to all-school samples and state-based decompositions (Tables A1–A3), Equation 1, and the standard-error method — all in an online supplement not available for this review, and all taken on trust here.

### Methods Review

**Rating:** Adequate (low confidence)  
**Internal confidence estimate:** 0.60

This is a descriptive study built on near-universe administrative data (CRDC, CCD, SEDA), and its core product is sound: student-weighted Black–White and Hispanic–White gaps in high-school security staffing, split into security guards (SSGs) and sworn officers (LEOs). The main takeaways are well supported: gaps are positive, SSGs drive them, and the Black–White gap is concentrated between districts within metro areas. The finer points are less secure. The between-region component is a large, unestimated residual that the paper nonetheless reads as substantive. The RQ3 claim that "segregation is the only significant predictor" rests on regressions the paper does not report. Several data-handling and inference details (missing-data treatment, standard errors, the decomposition equation) are either absent from the main text or deferred to an online appendix that was not available for this review.

**Strengths:**

- [JUDGMENT] The design fits the question. The research questions are explicitly descriptive (p.3), and the paper mostly avoids causal language about the effects of security personnel, noting that "no rigorous causal evidence" exists on SSGs (text, p.2).
- [JUDGMENT] Splitting SSGs from LEOs is the paper's main contribution, and it holds up. In Table 1 (p.7), the Black–White SSG gap (0.974 in 2018) is more than five times the LEO gap (0.172), and the Hispanic–White overall LEO gap is not significant in 2018 (0.026, p = 0.158). A reader who only knew the officer-focused literature would have a different picture.
- [JUDGMENT] The exposure measure is student-weighted and counts staffing intensity (FTE per 1,000 students), not just presence (text, p.5). That fits the claim about what students encounter better than prevalence measures do. Weighting by group enrollment also keeps small schools with extreme per-capita rates from dominating.
- [CHECKABLE] The text's headline numbers match Table 1 (p.7): 1.163 → 1.021 Black–White overall (change p = 0.110); 0.792 → 0.656 Hispanic–White (change p = 0.040); a between-district/within-CBSA component of 0.944 and 0.832, which is 81% and 81.5% of the respective overall gaps, consistent with "roughly 80%" (text, p.8). The between-region residuals in Table 1 equal the overall gap minus the four estimated components, to rounding, in all 12 columns.
- [JUDGMENT] Robustness to the unit of analysis (all schools, and states instead of CBSAs) is claimed in Supplemental Tables A1–A3 (text, p.8). That is the right set of checks, but the tables are **not available** for verification here.

**Weaknesses:**

- [CHECKABLE] The multivariate regression behind the RQ3 conclusion ("racial segregation is the strongest and only significant predictor," text, p.10) appears in no table or figure in the article. The text does not point to an appendix table for it either; the only appendix reference in that paragraph is Figure A1, for LEOs. No coefficients, standard errors, number of CBSAs, weights, or year are reported. Figure 2 (p.11) shows bivariate fits only.
- [CHECKABLE] The between-region component is large (−0.356 Black–White and −0.295 Hispanic–White for total personnel in 2018; Table 1, p.7). The Table 1 note says it "is the residual of the overall gap minus the sum of the gaps at each geographic scale and is not estimated," and it has no p-value. The text (pp.8, 10) still interprets it substantively, as regions with more students of color staffing fewer personnel, and describes a "paradox."
- [JUDGMENT] Because that residual is about a third of the Black–White gap, the four estimated components sum to about 130% of the overall gap (0.014 + 0.303 + 0.944 + 0.258 = 1.519 vs. 1.163; Table 1, p.7). So "80% of the gap" (p.8) is a share of a net total that includes offsetting pieces, not a clean attribution. I could not easily reconcile a residual of this size with the regional means in Figure 1 (p.9). The SSG means shown there run from about 0.34 (South) to about 1.28 (Northeast), and only the Northeast is above about 0.62. The residual may therefore also be absorbing things like CBSAs that cross division or region lines, schools outside any CBSA, or estimation discrepancies. The decomposition equation is **not available**, so I cannot determine which.
- [CHECKABLE] In the overall rows of Table 1 (p.7), the SSG and LEO columns do not sum to the total-personnel column in three of four cases: Black–White 2018, 0.974 + 0.172 = 1.146 vs. 1.163; Black–White 2021, 0.823 + 0.179 = 1.002 vs. 1.021; Hispanic–White 2018, 0.749 + 0.026 = 0.775 vs. 0.792. The text repeats this ("Of this total [1.16], 0.97 ... were SSGs and 0.17 were LEOs," p.6) without explaining the difference (for example, separate winsorizing or other personnel categories).
- [CHECKABLE] Figure 1 (p.9) is described inconsistently. The text (p.8) and the caption formula (Black_r/ΣBlack_r) describe the x-axis as each region's share of the *national* Black or Hispanic student population. But the axis label and title say "percent of high school students in [the] Census region" who are Black or Hispanic. The plotted Panel A values (about 0.05, 0.135, 0.14, 0.23) sum to about 0.56, which is impossible for national shares across the four regions, so the axis appears to show within-region composition.
- [CHECKABLE] The text says Figure 1 shows "a clear downward slope: regions with larger minority shares staff fewer security personnel" (p.8). But in Panel A (Black) the LEO fit line slopes *upward* (from about 0.25 for the West to about 0.53 for the South), and each panel has only N = 4 points (Figure 1 note, p.9).
- [CHECKABLE] The racial-composition predictor is defined as "the proportion of non-White students" (text, p.6), but Figure 2's Panels B and E (p.11) plot "Black Enrollment Share" and "Hispanic Enrollment Share." Figure 2's caption refers to SSG gaps, while its y-axes read "Difference in Exposure to Security." The survey year behind Figure 2, and the number of CBSAs plotted, are not reported.
- [CHECKABLE] Missing-data handling is not described. The text reports "around 3% of total observations" missing security-personnel data across the two waves, with NYC Public Schools' 2017–18 staffing data affected by a submission error, and "approximately 5%" missing in 2020–21 (pp.4–5). It does not say whether missing schools were dropped or imputed, or whether NYC is included in either wave.
- [JUDGMENT] Leaving out NYC matters more than the 3% figure suggests. It is the largest district in the country and enrolls large numbers of Black and Hispanic high-school students, and dropping it in one wave but not the other would also contaminate the 2018→2021 comparisons.
- [CHECKABLE] The paper never mentions COVID-19 or the pandemic, although one of its two waves is 2020–21 (the words do not appear in the text). FRPL-based poverty measures (note 3, p.12) and FTE staffing counts in that year may reflect remote/hybrid operations and meal-program waivers.
- [CHECKABLE] Poverty is described as "free lunch program eligibility" (p.5) but measured as "free or reduced-price lunch (FRPL)" (note 3, p.12).
- [CHECKABLE] The high-school analytic sample size, the definition of a "high school" (grade span), the CRDC–CCD–SEDA match rates, and how non-CBSA (rural) schools enter the nested decomposition are not reported in the main text. The only sample size given is "about 80,000 schools each year" for all schools (p.5).
- [CHECKABLE] The text standardizes the LEO gap as "about 0.26 standard deviation units" (p.6) but never reports the LEO mean or SD. The reported SSG mean of 1.11 (SD = 2.15, p.6) is not defined: school-weighted or student-weighted, and which year.
- [JUDGMENT] Standard errors, the clustering level, and the regression (Equation 1) that generates every p-value in Table 1 are deferred to the Supplemental Appendix and are **not available**. With 9 divisions and 4 regions, inference on the higher-level components depends heavily on how dependence is modeled. Readers cannot judge this from the article.
- [JUDGMENT] The RQ3 conclusions (p.10) go well beyond the evidence: SSG deployment "operate[s] independently of racial composition or poverty concentration once segregation is accounted for," and "LEO placement follows entirely different mechanisms." They rest on a cross-sectional regression across CBSAs with three predictors that are strongly related to each other, and the regression is not shown. Nonsignificance there is not independence. There is also a mechanical link. Within-CBSA exposure gaps cannot exist without between-school segregation, as the paper itself notes ("a necessary but not sufficient component," p.6). So a positive segregation–gap association is partly built in, and racial differences in exposure to poverty also depend on segregation.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Rely on the RQ1 magnitudes in Table 1 (p.7) as solid descriptive facts, conditional on CRDC reporting: Black students in high school attend schools with about 1.0–1.2 more security FTE per 1,000 students than White students, and Hispanic students about 0.66–0.79 more, mostly SSGs.
- Treat the SSG/LEO split as the durable contribution. The Black–White LEO gap is real but small (0.17–0.18; Table 1). Among Hispanic students there is no positive LEO gap: 0.026 (p = 0.158) in 2018 and −0.055 in 2021.
- The abstract says disparities are "present across all geographic scales and for LEOs." Read that narrowly. In Table 1, no within-region/between-division component is significant (all p ≥ 0.76), and the Hispanic–White LEO gap is not positive.
- Read the between-district/within-CBSA finding (0.944 of 1.163 for Black–White in 2018; Table 1) as "most of the disparity is visible when comparing districts in the same metro area." Do not read it as "district policy choices cause 80% of the gap." The design cannot separate district allocation decisions from sorting of students across districts. The text's attribution to "district-level choices" (p.10) is an interpretation, not an estimate.
- Do not build on the negative between-region component or the regional "paradox" (pp.8, 10). It is an unestimated residual with no standard error (Table 1 note, p.7), its size is hard to reconcile with Figure 1's regional means, and Figure 1 rests on four points with an inconsistently defined x-axis.
- Treat the RQ3 result that "segregation is the only significant predictor" (p.10) as unverified until you have seen the multivariate estimates. Figure 2 supports only the bivariate claim that CBSA gaps rise with segregation and with poverty-exposure differences, and are flat or slightly declining in minority enrollment share.
- Be careful with 2018→2021 changes. One is statistically significant but unremarked: the Black–White SSG gap falls from 0.974 to 0.823 (p = 0.035; Table 1). It could reflect pandemic-year operations, post-2020 staffing changes, or NYC reporting differences, not real reallocation. The paper's suggestion that districts may be swapping SSGs for LEOs (p.10) is not tested.
- Before citing the robustness claims (all schools; state instead of CBSA), check Supplemental Tables A1–A3 yourself. They were not available for this review.

**Detailed Commentary:**

*Design and estimand.* The paper sets out to describe, not to estimate causal effects, and it largely stays in that lane in the RQ1–RQ2 results. The estimand is the difference in the average school-level staffing rate experienced by the typical Black (or Hispanic) and the typical White high-school student (text, p.5). It is a standard exposure-gap construction, following Goldhaber et al. (2015), and it suits a policy audience asking "who is around more security staff." Readers should keep three limits in mind. First, it measures staffing, not contact: all students in a school are treated as equally exposed, and the paper acknowledges that encounter frequency is not measured (p.5). Second, the per-1,000 scaling means school size affects the rate. If Black and Hispanic students attend larger high schools on average, the per-capita measure could understate or overstate what individual students experience, depending on how security scales with enrollment. Third, CRDC reports FTE counts by type but not roles or duties, so an SSG in one district may do very different work than an SSG in another. The paper's framing of SSGs as possibly amplifying or reducing the school-to-prison pathway (p.2) should be read with that in mind.

*Data.* The sources are credible and close to universal, which is the paper's biggest data advantage. The weak spots are in how the data are handled, and the main text says too little about each. The missing-data paragraph (pp.4–5) spends its words justifying why missingness is not worrying rather than saying what was done with it. It reports about 3% missing across both waves and about 5% in 2020–21 without saying whether those schools are dropped. Missingness concentrated in NYC's 2017–18 security staffing is exactly the case where "3% of observations" understates the potential effect on a student-weighted Black–White or Hispanic–White gap. Winsorizing at three times the 99th percentile (p.5) is light, and weighting by enrollment limits the damage extreme small-school values can do. But note 1 (p.12) ends with the odd claim that the authors have "no reason to believe the winsorized staffing values are erroneous," which sits awkwardly next to the decision to winsorize them. The 2020–21 wave is a pandemic year, and the paper never discusses that. This matters little for the within-year cross-sectional patterns, which look very similar across waves in Table 1. It matters more for any reading of change over time.

*The decomposition.* The nested decomposition (region → division → CBSA → district → school) is a sensible way to answer RQ2, and the estimated components are internally consistent in Table 1 (the residual identity holds in every column). Two issues limit it. First, the between-region piece is a residual rather than an estimate (Table 1 note, p.7), and it is large and negative. Because of that, the positive estimated components add up to well over 100% of the overall gap, so statements like "roughly 80% of the total gap" (p.8) describe a share of a net figure with offsetting parts. Second, the geography does not nest cleanly. The paper notes that CBSAs can cross state lines (p.6), and some cross division or region lines. About 5% of the population lives outside any CBSA (p.6). The main text does not say how either case is handled, and a residual component is where such problems would show up. I also could not reconcile a between-region SSG component of −0.363 with Figure 1's regional SSG means, which appear to range from about 0.34 to 1.28 with only the Northeast above about 0.62. The paper's reported mean SSG exposure of 1.11 (p.6) is also hard to square with those regional means if both are student-weighted. Figure 1 may be computed on a different basis, and this is a judgment about apparent inconsistency, not a demonstrated error. Figure 1 itself is illustrative at best: four points, a weighted fit line, and an x-axis whose description in the text and caption formula (national share) disagrees with its axis label and plotted values (within-region share).

*Inference.* Every p-value in Table 1 comes from "Equation (1)" in the Supplemental Appendix (Table 1 note, p.7), which is **not available**. So I cannot assess clustering, whether the two waves are treated as a panel of mostly the same schools when testing changes, or how uncertainty is defined for data that cover nearly the whole population. The pattern of p-values looks plausible (very large p-values for the within-region/between-division components, very small ones for the district and school components), but readers should not treat the between-year tests as more than rough guides. One text-to-table discrepancy is worth noting. The Hispanic–White LEO gap is described as "slightly negative in 2021 (p = .001)" (pp.6–8), but in Table 1 the 0.001 is the p-value for the change from 2018. The test against zero is reported as 0.000.

*RQ3.* This is the weakest part of the paper methodologically. Figure 2 (p.11) shows CBSA-level bivariate scatters with linear and quadratic fits. The positive association between segregation and the SSG gap in Panels A and D is visible and credible as description. But the paper's strongest conclusions, (a)–(c) on p.10, depend on a multivariate regression that is not reported anywhere in the article. Even taken at face value, those conclusions infer mechanisms from a cross-sectional regression across CBSAs. The segregation index and the racial difference in poverty exposure are closely linked by construction, since both require between-school sorting. Segregation is also partly a precondition for the outcome, since within-CBSA exposure gaps cannot exist without it. "Only significant predictor" in that setting says little about whether poverty concentration or composition matter. The claim that LEO placement "follows entirely different mechanisms" rests on nonsignificance in Figure A1, which is **not available**. There are also smaller inconsistencies: the composition variable is defined as the non-White share on p.6 but plotted as the Black or Hispanic share; the year, the number of CBSAs, and whether the outcome is the SSG gap or the total-personnel gap are not stated for Figure 2.

*Bottom line for readers.* The paper reliably shows that Black and, to a lesser extent, Hispanic high-school students attend schools with more security staffing than White students. It shows that guards, not sworn officers, account for most of this, and that for Black–White gaps most of it is visible between districts within metro areas. Those findings are useful for the police-free-schools debate the authors target. The regional "paradox," the exact attribution percentages, the changes between waves, and especially the RQ3 claims about mechanisms should be treated as suggestive at most until the appendix materials and unreported estimates are checked.

---

### Literature Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)  
**Internal confidence estimate:** 0.70

The Brief places itself well within the segregation and school-resource-distribution literature, the authors' home ground, and it correctly identifies school security guards (SSGs) as an understudied part of school security. Its account of the school-policing and school-security literature is thinner and less reliable. At least two citations about the prior evidence base appear to be mischaracterized. The claim that earlier distributional work "focused exclusively on LEOs" leaves out a criminology and sociology literature, based on the School Survey on Crime and Safety (SSOCS), that has examined security guards and other security measures by school racial composition for more than a decade. Readers can rely on the paper for its new descriptive decomposition. They should not rely on it as a map of what is already known about security guards or about the causal effects of police in schools.

**Strengths:**

- **[CHECKABLE]** The spatial framing draws on the right segregation literature: multilevel and geographic-scale segregation (Fischer et al., 2004; Reardon et al., 2008; A. Owens et al., 2016; Jang, 2024) and segregation-linked resource inequality (Sosina & Weathers, 2019; Weathers & Sosina, 2022; Lee et al., 2022). These works are cited on p.4 to motivate why geographic units could mediate exposure.
- **[CHECKABLE]** The paper cites the most important recent quasi-experimental study of school resource officers (Sorensen et al., 2023, JPAM; p.2) and the closest prior study that treats SSGs separately from sworn officers (Vernon & Curran, 2024, *Criminology & Public Policy*; p.2).
- **[CHECKABLE]** The decomposition approach is tied explicitly to an earlier use in education research (Goldhaber et al., 2015; text, p.5), and the prevalence-versus-exposure distinction is explained with reference to earlier CRDC-based work (Lindsay et al., 2018; Gleit, 2022; pp.3–4).
- **[JUDGMENT]** The introduction connects a fast-moving policy setting (police-free schools, Chicago's removal of officers while keeping security staff, state SRO mandates) to a real empirical gap. The Chicago example (text, p.2) gives a concrete reason why distinguishing SSGs from LEOs matters.
- **[JUDGMENT]** The paper is candid that "no rigorous causal evidence" exists on SSGs' effects (text, p.2). As far as I know, that is accurate, and the paper keeps its contribution descriptive.

**Weaknesses:**

- **[CHECKABLE]** On p.2 the paper states that "correlational evidence supports the latter" (that SSGs may *attenuate* the school-to-prison nexus) and cites E. G. Owens (2017). **[JUDGMENT]** To my knowledge, Owens (2017, JPAM, "Testing the School-to-Prison Pipeline") is not about security guards. It studies sworn police in schools using variation from federal COPS hiring grants, which is a quasi-experimental design, not a correlational one. Its main findings, as I recall them, are that police in schools raise law enforcement's detection of school crime and increase arrests of young children. If anything, that is evidence *for* the pipeline concern, not against it. This citation is mismatched on subject, design, and direction of the finding.
- **[CHECKABLE]** On p.2 the paper states that "quasi-experimental studies show that exposure to LEOs disproportionately affects the likelihood of arrests for Black students" and cites Pigott et al. (2018) and Sorensen et al. (2023). **[CHECKABLE]** The reference-list title of Pigott et al. (2018) is about "discovering trends of expulsions" (p.14), not arrests. **[JUDGMENT]** I am not confident Pigott et al. uses a quasi-experimental design. My recollection is that Sorensen et al. (2023) finds the clearest racially disproportionate effects on exclusionary discipline, with the arrest evidence weaker. Readers should check both before repeating the sentence.
- **[CHECKABLE]** On p.2 the paper says that "qualitative evidence supports the first case" (SSGs reinforcing carceral logics) and cites Mallett (2016). **[CHECKABLE]** The reference list describes Mallett (2016) as "a critical review" of the school-to-prison pipeline (p.13). **[JUDGMENT]** A narrative review of the pipeline is not qualitative evidence about security guards. Actual ethnographic work on non-sworn school security staff exists (see Guidance) and is not cited.
- **[CHECKABLE]** On p.3 the paper states that "Prior studies addressing racial/ethnic inequality in prevalence and exposure to school policing have focused exclusively on LEOs," and on p.4 it presents SSG inclusion as the first "notable gap." **[CHECKABLE]** The reference list contains no SSOCS-based or NCES *Indicators of School Crime and Safety* work, and no study of security measures by school racial composition other than the police-focused CRDC pieces. **[JUDGMENT]** There is a sizable literature, mostly in criminology and sociology and mostly using SSOCS, that examines security guards together with other security measures by the racial and poverty composition of schools. This makes the novelty claim too broad as stated. What is new is the CRDC-based, FTE-per-student *exposure* measure for SSGs and its geographic decomposition, not attention to guards as such.
- **[CHECKABLE]** RQ3 tests "racial threat dynamics" using CBSA-level racial composition (text, p.6) and cites only Eitle et al. (2002), a general social-control study that is not about schools. **[CHECKABLE]** Irwin et al. (2022), which argues "against racial threat and toward a racial control perspective" for school punishment (reference title, p.13), is cited only for the claim that the police-free schools movement "helped fuel institutional conversations" (p.2). **[JUDGMENT]** The school-specific racial-threat literature (Welch & Payne and related work) is missing. The paper also does not engage with Irwin et al.'s actual argument, even though RQ3's result (segregation, not composition, predicts the CBSA gap; text, p.10) looks more like a racial-control account than a racial-threat account.
- **[CHECKABLE]** The causal SRO literature cited is limited to Pigott et al. (2018) and Sorensen et al. (2023) on p.2, plus Fisher & Hennessy (2016), a meta-analysis cited only for the historical rise of security after shootings (pp.1–2). **[JUDGMENT]** Several well-known quasi-experimental or panel studies of police in schools are not cited (e.g., Weisburst, 2019; Gottfredson et al., 2020; Na & Gottfredson, 2013). The paper therefore gives readers a one-sided picture: LEOs are described as a "well-documented and understood" step in the pipeline (p.2), but the causal evidence is more mixed on safety outcomes and more consistent on discipline.
- **[CHECKABLE]** Several factual statements have no citation: the "30,000 FTE SSGs compared to 22,000 FTE SROs" comparison (p.4; no CRDC year given, and the wording switches between "LEOs" and "SROs"); the "ongoing rise in high-profile school shootings" (p.3); and the claim that unequal SSG exposure may "affect students' sense of safety and belonging" (p.3). **[JUDGMENT]** A relevant empirical literature on visible security and student perceptions exists and could have supported or qualified the last claim.
- **[CHECKABLE]** On p.3, Sorensen et al. (2023) is cited for the claim that SSG staffing "is usually governed by district-level policy and budget decisions." **[JUDGMENT]** Sorensen et al. is an SRO study. Readers should check whether it actually addresses how SSGs are staffed.
- **[CHECKABLE]** The words "COVID" and "pandemic" do not appear anywhere in the paper, although one of the two data waves is 2020–21. **[JUDGMENT]** The 2018–2021 comparisons in Table 1 (p.7) therefore come with no literature or context on pandemic-era operations and staffing, which readers need for interpreting any change over time.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- **Before repeating citations about the prior evidence base, verify them.** Specifically: (a) E. G. Owens (2017) as evidence that SSGs attenuate the pipeline (p.2). I believe it is a quasi-experimental study of police, not guards. (b) Pigott et al. (2018) as quasi-experimental evidence on arrests of Black students (p.2). Its title concerns expulsions. (c) Mallett (2016) as "qualitative evidence" (p.2). It is a critical review. (d) Sorensen et al. (2023) as a source on SSG staffing (p.3). (e) Maryland's Safe to Learn Act as requiring LEOs in "all public schools" (p.3). My recollection, which I am unsure of, is that the mandate covers public high schools and allows "adequate local law enforcement coverage" as an alternative.
- **For earlier work on security guards and security measures by race (the SSOCS tradition), consult these.** I am confident these lines of work exist but less sure of every bibliographic detail. Nance (2016, *Washington University Law Review*, "Students, Police, and the School-to-Prison Pipeline") and Nance (2017, *Emory Law Journal*, on student surveillance and racial inequalities) show that schools with more students of color use more intense surveillance and security after conditioning on crime and disorder. Kupchik & Ward (2014, *Youth Violence and Juvenile Justice*) examine race, poverty, and school security measures across school levels. Servoss & Finn (2014) and Finn & Servoss (2014) relate security measures to school racial composition. Steinka-Fry, Fisher & Tanner-Smith (2016) develop typologies of visible security measures, including guards. NCES's annual *Indicators of School Crime and Safety* reports the presence of "security guards or security personnel" separately from sworn officers, broken down by school characteristics. These studies mostly measure *prevalence* (any guard present), not the per-student *exposure* this paper measures. That difference is what the paper actually adds.
- **For qualitative and ethnographic work on non-sworn security staff:** Nolan (2011, *Police in the Hallways*) on New York City's School Safety Agents; Devine (1996, *Maximum Security*) on security staff in New York City high schools; and Kupchik (2010, *Homeroom Security*). These address the question the paper calls open (what guards actually do) and show that "SSG" covers very different roles. NYC's School Safety Agents are NYPD employees with peace-officer status, which blurs the CRDC's LEO/SSG line. That matters here because the paper reports that New York City's 2017–18 security data were problematic (text, p.4).
- **For the causal evidence on police in schools, which the paper's single-sentence summary on p.2 does not cover:** Weisburst (2019, JPAM) uses Texas COPS grants and finds higher discipline and worse long-run educational attainment. Gottfredson et al. (2020, *Criminology & Public Policy*) find that SRO grants in Pennsylvania increased recorded offenses and exclusionary responses. Na & Gottfredson (2013, *Justice Quarterly*) use SSOCS panel data. Sorensen et al. (2023) also report reductions in some forms of school violence alongside the discipline increases. That trade-off is the relevant "conflicting evidence," and the paper does not mention it.
- **For the pipeline mechanism itself:** economics now offers causal evidence on the discipline-to-crime link, e.g., Bacher-Hicks, Billings & Deming's work on the long-run effects of school suspensions on adult crime (NBER working paper around 2019, possibly published later; I am unsure of the final venue). This literature supports the premise that exposure to security personnel matters only insofar as it changes discipline. The paper's own results cannot establish that.
- **For racial threat versus racial control:** the school-specific racial-threat studies by Welch & Payne (e.g., 2010, *Social Problems*) and Payne & Welch (2010, *Criminology*) measure composition at the school level. The paper tests composition at the CBSA level against CBSA-level gaps (text, p.6; Figure 2, p.11). Its null result for composition is therefore not a direct test of the school-level racial-threat hypothesis. Read Irwin et al. (2022) for the alternative framework the paper's findings seem to fit better.
- **How to cite this paper relative to its antecedents.** Cite it for: (1) national CRDC-based estimates of Black–White and Hispanic–White gaps in per-student *exposure* to SSGs versus LEOs in high schools (Table 1, p.7); (2) the finding that the Black–White gap is concentrated between districts within CBSAs (about 0.94 of 1.16 FTE per 1,000 in 2017–18; Table 1, p.7; text, p.8); and (3) the bivariate CBSA-level association between segregation and SSG gaps (Figure 2, p.11). The multivariate RQ3 regression the text describes (p.10) is not reported in the main text, and the LEO analogue (Figure A1) is not available. For the observation that schools serving students of color have more guards and surveillance *in general*, cite the SSOCS-based literature above. For LEO prevalence patterns, cite Gleit (2022) and Sorensen et al. (2023) directly. For the level-of-governance decomposition logic, the closest methodological sibling is arguably Lee, Shores & Williams (2022), co-authored by one of this paper's authors, as well as Goldhaber et al. (2015).
- The technical details of the decomposition estimator (Supplemental Appendix Equation 1) and the robustness tables A1–A3 are **not available** to me. Nothing in this review depends on them.

**Detailed Commentary:**

*Coverage.* The paper draws on two literatures and handles them unevenly. The segregation and resource-inequality literature is covered well and used for a specific purpose: to motivate decomposing exposure gaps by geographic scale and to interpret the negative between-region residual as reflecting interregional funding differences (text, p.8, citing Lee et al., 2022). **[CHECKABLE]** Four of the roughly 37 references are co-authored by members of the author team (Lee et al., 2022; Sosina & Weathers, 2019; Weathers & Sosina, 2022; Reardon et al., 2024), all in this segregation and resource thread. That is normal and appropriate. The school security literature is thinner. **[CHECKABLE]** Many of its citations are news stories, an Urban Institute blog post, statutes, or government guidance (e.g., Richards, 2020; Pendharkar, 2023; Franza & Perlman, 2024; Lindsay et al., 2018; the Maryland, Texas, and Wisconsin statutes; U.S. DOJ COPS, 2022). The peer-reviewed empirical core on school security consists of Gleit (2022), Sorensen et al. (2023), Vernon & Curran (2024), Pigott et al. (2018), E. G. Owens (2017), and Fisher & Hennessy (2016). **[JUDGMENT]** For a Brief, a compressed review is expected. But the omissions are concentrated where the paper makes its novelty claim, which makes them more consequential than their number suggests.

*Accuracy of characterization.* The most consequential problem is the paragraph on p.2 that sets up the theory of SSGs' "contradictory influences." It assigns one strand of evidence to each side: qualitative evidence (Mallett, 2016) for the reinforcing role and correlational evidence (E. G. Owens, 2017) for the attenuating role. **[JUDGMENT]** Based on my knowledge of both works, neither fits its label. Mallett is a review of the pipeline literature, not a qualitative study of guards. Owens is a quasi-experimental study of sworn police whose findings, as I understand them, point toward *more* formal processing of young students, not less. If that is right, the paper's "balanced" framing of SSGs has no empirical support on the attenuating side beyond the qualitative interview study of security professionals (Forber-Pratt et al., 2023) and whatever Vernon & Curran (2024) find. I am confident about Owens (2017)'s subject and design. I am less certain of Pigott et al. (2018)'s design, so I flag it for verification rather than as an error. I also cannot verify the paper's summary of Gleit (2022) on differential officer roles by school racial composition (p.4). It is plausible, and readers wanting that specific claim should go to Gleit directly.

*Novelty.* **[JUDGMENT]** The strongest defensible novelty claim is narrower than the one the paper makes. SSOCS-based studies, the NCES *Indicators* reports, and legal scholarship (notably Nance) have documented that schools serving more students of color are more likely to have security guards and other surveillance measures, often after accounting for reported crime and disorder. What those studies did not do, and this paper does, is (a) use the CRDC universe, which is not a sample, (b) measure staffing intensity per 1,000 students rather than presence, (c) separate guards from sworn officers in a common exposure metric, and (d) decompose the national gap by geographic scale. Point (d) is the real contribution, and the finding that the Black–White gap mostly arises between districts within metro areas (Table 1, p.7) has no close precedent that I know of. The paper would be better cited for these specific contributions than for being the first to look beyond police. One tension within the paper is worth noting. **[CHECKABLE]** It describes Vernon & Curran (2024) in its reference list as examining "the relationship between school security guards, school resource officers, and student behavior, discipline, and arrests" (p.14) while stating on p.3 that prior prevalence and exposure studies focused "exclusively" on LEOs. The two statements are compatible only if "prior studies" means distributional studies specifically. Readers should keep that narrow reading in mind.

*Conflicting evidence.* **[JUDGMENT]** The paper does not engage evidence that cuts against a purely inequity-based reading of security staffing. Two strands matter. First, part of the causal SRO literature finds safety benefits alongside discipline costs; Sorensen et al. (2023), cited here only for the discipline side, is an example. A reader who takes in only the p.2 sentence will not know that trade-off exists. Second, the SSOCS literature has long debated how much security deployment tracks school crime, disorder, size, and urbanicity rather than racial composition, and some studies (e.g., work by Kupchik and colleagues, as I recall) find that poverty or urbanicity accounts for much of the raw racial pattern. The paper's own decomposition places most of the gap *between* districts within CBSAs (Table 1, p.7). That is exactly where differences in urbanicity, district size, and reported incident rates, which the paper itself lists as SRO placement criteria on p.3, would appear. The paper states that disparities reflect "district-level choices about how security staff is allocated" (text, p.10). The literature it omits would give readers reason to treat that as one hypothesis among several.

*Placement in adjacent fields.* **[JUDGMENT]** Sociology of education and segregation research: well integrated. Criminology (racial threat, the school security measures literature, SRO evaluations): underused, even though RQ3 is in effect a criminological hypothesis test. Economics of education: represented by Sorensen et al. (2023) and E. G. Owens (2017), though the latter is mis-described. The long-run causal evidence on discipline and crime, and the Weisburst (2019) evidence on police funding, are absent. Developmental and school psychology: the only engagement is Forber-Pratt et al. (2023). The literature on how visible security affects students' perceived safety, belonging, and fear (for example, Tanner-Smith & Fisher and colleagues, and Mowen and colleagues; I am confident this literature exists but less sure of individual titles) would give readers a way to judge whether the SSG exposure gaps documented here are likely to matter for students. Qualitative traditions: largely missing. There is ethnographic work on non-sworn security staff in urban high schools (Devine, 1996; Nolan, 2011), and it complicates the paper's clean LEO/SSG distinction. That matters because the paper relies on the CRDC's definitions (text, p.2) and because New York City, whose School Safety Agents are the most prominent hybrid case, is also the district with the documented CRDC reporting problem (text, p.4).

*Limits of this review.* I have not searched the literature for this review. My statements about outside works come from my own training knowledge. I am most confident about E. G. Owens (2017), Sorensen et al. (2023), Weisburst (2019), Gottfredson et al. (2020), Nance's work, and the existence of the SSOCS security-measures literature. I am less confident about exact titles, years, and venues for several of the criminology citations (Kupchik & Ward, 2014; Servoss & Finn, 2014; Steinka-Fry et al., 2016), about Pigott et al. (2018)'s design, and about the details of Gleit (2022). Readers should confirm bibliographic details before relying on them. I also cannot assess any literature discussion that might appear in the online Supplemental Appendix, which is not available.
