### Writing Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)  
**Internal confidence estimate:** 0.72

This brief is clearly organized around three explicit research questions, and for RQ1 and RQ2 its Results prose reproduces the numbers in Table 1 (p.7) accurately at the stated rounding. Fidelity weakens toward the end. The RQ3 conclusions about segregation "once segregation is accounted for" rest on multivariate regressions that appear in no exhibit. Figure 1 (p.9) defines its x-axis in two incompatible ways and supports a weaker pattern than the prose describes. The abstract and several interpretive sentences also describe disparities as "present across all geographic scales," "structural," and the product of district "choices," which goes beyond what the descriptive decomposition shows. Readers can trust the reported gap magnitudes, but they should re-read the interpretive sentences against Table 1 before citing them.

**Strengths:**

- [JUDGMENT] The structure is easy to navigate. The three RQs are numbered on p.3, and the Results subsections on pp.6–10 are headed to match them one-to-one, so a reader can find the evidence for each question quickly.
- [CHECKABLE] The headline numbers in the RQ1 and RQ2 prose match Table 1 (p.7) at two-decimal rounding. Examples: 1.16 vs 1.163, 1.02 vs 1.021, 0.79 vs 0.792, 0.66 vs 0.656, 0.94 vs 0.944, 0.83 vs 0.832, 0.48/0.49 vs 0.476/0.491. The p-values quoted in the text for the aggregate gaps (p = .110 and p = .04 for changes, p < .001 for 2021 levels; text, p.6) match Table 1's first and second 2021 p-values.
- [CHECKABLE] The Table 1 note (p.7) explains its dual p-value convention for 2021 (first p-value tests 2021 vs 2018, second tests 2021 vs zero). It also states that the between-region row is a residual that "is not estimated," which is an honest disclosure that a careful reader needs.
- [JUDGMENT] The terminology section (pp.2–3) usefully explains the CRDC distinction between SSGs and LEOs, and why SROs and SPOs are pooled. The exposure-versus-prevalence distinction (pp.3–5) is well motivated.
- [JUDGMENT] The Discussion mostly hedges its policy extrapolations ("may still leave," "One possibility is," p.10).

**Weaknesses:**

- [CHECKABLE] **RQ3's central claim has no exhibit.** The text (p.10) says "multivariate regression results reveal that racial segregation is the strongest and only significant predictor." It then concludes that SSG patterns "operate independently of racial composition or poverty concentration once segregation is accounted for." No coefficient, standard error, N, or model specification for this regression appears in the main text. The appendix exhibits the paper lists (Tables A1–A3, Figure A1; pp.6, 8, 10) do not include it either, as they are described. Figure 2 (p.11) is explicitly "bivariate" (note, p.11). Whether the regressions are in the appendix is not available to this reviewer.
- [CHECKABLE] **Figure 1's x-axis is defined in two incompatible ways.** The title (p.9) says "percent of the Census region that is Black or Hispanic," and the axis labels read "Percent of High School Students in Census Region: Black/Hispanic." The note's formula, Black_r / ΣBlack_r, instead defines a region's share of the *national* Black population, and the text (p.8) likewise says "its share of the national Black (Panel A) or Hispanic (Panel B) student population." The plotted Panel A values (roughly West 0.05, Midwest 0.14, Northeast 0.14, South 0.23) sum to about 0.56, not 1, so they cannot be national shares. The formula in the note and the prose description therefore appear to be wrong. The axis is also labeled "Percent" but scaled as proportions (0.05–0.25).
- [CHECKABLE] **Figure 1 does not show a "clear downward slope" for every series.** The text (p.8) says the figure reveals "a clear downward slope: regions with larger minority shares staff fewer security personnel." The figure has N = 4 regions (note, p.9), shows no uncertainty, and fits lines "weighted by the percent of high school students in the region who are Black or Hispanic," so it is weighted by the x-variable itself. In Panel A the LEO line slopes *upward* (from about 0.23 at West to about 0.53 at South). The two extreme regions on the x-axis have nearly identical combined staffing (West about 0.87, South about 0.90), so the downward LEO+SSG line depends on the Northeast point (about 1.69) and the weighting.
- [CHECKABLE] **A change p-value is reported as a level p-value.** The text (p.8) says Hispanic–White LEO gaps were "slightly negative in 2021 (p = .001)." In Table 1 (p.7) the entry is −0.055 (0.001; 0.000). Under the table's own note, .001 is the p-value for the 2018-to-2021 *change*, and the test against zero is 0.000.
- [CHECKABLE] **A significant change is not mentioned.** The Black–White SSG gap fell from 0.974 to 0.823 with a change p-value of 0.035 (Table 1, p.7). The prose (p.6) discusses only the non-significant decline in the combined gap (p = .110) and never mentions the significant SSG decline.
- [CHECKABLE] **Several overstatements go beyond Table 1:**
  - The abstract (p.1) says "disparities are present across all geographic scales and for LEOs." The within-region-between-division components are never significant (p = .934, .789, .858, .910, .835, .908 in 2018; Table 1, p.7).
  - Hispanic–White LEO gaps are not positive: 0.026 (p = .158) in 2018 and −0.055 in 2021 (Table 1, p.7).
  - The text (p.8) says gaps "remain at every other finer spatial level—division, CBSA, and district," but the division-level components are 0.014 (p = .934) and 0.015 (p = .910).
- [CHECKABLE] **Some prose claims describe levels that Table 1 does not contain:**
  - The Hispanic–White pattern is attributed to "broader, state-level factors" (p.8), but Table 1 has no state level. States appear only in Tables A2/A3, which are not available.
  - The "within those same regions" paradox (p.10) implies region-specific within-region gaps, but Table 1 reports only national aggregates of each component.
- [CHECKABLE] **The subtype columns do not add up to the combined column, and the text never explains why.** SSG + LEO does not equal the combined "school security personnel" column in Table 1 (p.7): 0.974 + 0.172 = 1.146 vs 1.163 (B–W 2018); 0.823 + 0.179 = 1.002 vs 1.021 (B–W 2021); 0.749 + 0.026 = 0.775 vs 0.792 (H–W 2018). The prose repeats this non-additivity without comment: "Of this total [1.16], 0.97 … were SSGs and 0.17 were LEOs" (text, p.6).
- [CHECKABLE] **The analytic sample is not reported.** The number of high schools, districts, and CBSAs in the high-school analysis is never stated. The only counts given are "about 80,000 schools each year from nearly 13,000 school districts" (p.5), which describes the full dataset. Table 1 reports no N, and Figure 2 does not report the number of CBSAs.
- [CHECKABLE] **The paper's two descriptions of the racial-composition predictor disagree.** It is defined as "the proportion of non-White students" (p.6), but Figure 2 plots "Black Enrollment Share" and "Hispanic Enrollment Share" (Panels B and E, p.11).
- [JUDGMENT] **Mechanism language outruns the descriptive design.** Examples include "the disparity mainly arises from … district and metropolitan variation" and "structural inequalities in … deployment" (abstract, p.1). Others are "district-level choices" (p.10), "fundamentally associated with structural segregation" (p.10), and "LEO placement follows entirely different mechanisms" (p.10). The last is inferred from a non-significant result in Figure A1 (not available).

**Guidance for Readers:**

- **Read Table 1 (p.7) itself; it carries the paper.** RQ1 and RQ2 rest entirely on it. The prose numbers for gap sizes and components can be quoted as written. For p-values, check which of the two 2021 values the text is quoting.
- **Treat "roughly 80% of the total gap" (p.8) with care.** The ratio is arithmetically right against the *net* gap (0.944/1.163 = 81%; 0.832/1.021 = 81%). However, the positive components together sum to 131% of the net gap in 2018 (1.519/1.163), and the negative between-region residual (−0.356) offsets the excess. Against the sum of positive components, the between-district share is about 62%. "Share of the gap" is not a well-defined partition here, so quote the per-1,000 values rather than percentage shares.
- **Treat the between-region row as an accounting residual, not an estimate.** It has no standard error, and the note says it "is not estimated." The substantive stories built on it (regional funding regimes, p.8; the "paradox," p.10) are interpretations.
- **Use Figure 1 (p.9) as an illustration only.** It has four points and no uncertainty, its x-axis definition conflicts with its note formula and with the text, and its LEO line in Panel A slopes the opposite way.
- **Do not cite the RQ3 multivariate claims (p.10) without seeing the regression table.** Figure 2 (p.11) supports only the bivariate statement that segregation and poverty-exposure gaps correlate positively with CBSA-level SSG gaps, while enrollment share is flat to slightly negative.
- **Before quoting a trend, check which changes were actually significant.** Table 1 shows three significant 2018-to-2021 changes:
  - B–W SSG decline (p = .035), which the prose omits.
  - H–W combined decline (p = .040), which the prose reports.
  - H–W LEO shift to negative (p = .001), which the prose mislabels as a level test.
  
  Note also that the significant Hispanic–White decline coincides with a significant LEO shift, while the SSG change is not significant (0.749 to 0.712, p = .511). This sits awkwardly with "entirely attributable to SSG exposure" (p.6).
- **The introduction (pp.1–4) can be skimmed** by readers who know the school-policing literature. The data paragraph on missingness (pp.4–5) is worth reading, because it does not say how missing schools were handled.
- **Anything about all-school samples, state-based decompositions, or the estimating equation is in the Supplemental Appendix, which is not available here.** The robustness claims on p.8 (patterns "quite consistent," "about 60% lower" exposure in all schools) cannot be checked from the article.

**Detailed Commentary:**

*Organization.* For a 14-page brief the paper is well sequenced: motivation, terminology, RQs (p.3), data and methods (pp.4–6), results by RQ (pp.6–10), and discussion (pp.10–12). The weak point is where the method lives. The decomposition estimator is described only verbally (p.5). The Table 1 note cites "Equation (1)," but the main text has no Equation (1), and the same note later refers to "Supplemental Appendix Equation 1." A reader of the article alone cannot see how components are estimated, why they are additive, or why the SSG and LEO columns do not add to the combined column. Table 1 also reports only point estimates with p-values: no standard errors, no N, and no mean exposure levels. The mean and SD of SSG exposure used for the effect-size conversions appear only in prose (p.6).

*Fidelity of argument.* The RQ1 and RQ2 narration tracks Table 1 closely. Drift appears in three places:

- **Interpretive glosses on the decomposition.** A between-district component is attributed to "district-level choices about how security staff is allocated across schools serving more Black and Hispanic students" (p.10). That sentence describes within-district allocation, which is the smaller component (0.258 vs 0.944 for B–W 2018, Table 1). It also calls a between-district difference a "choice."
- **The Hispanic–White "state-level" reading (p.8).** No state level appears in Table 1.
- **RQ3.** The three lettered conclusions on p.10 are phrased as mechanism claims ("fundamentally," "operate independently," "entirely different mechanisms"), but the only visible evidence is six bivariate scatterplots. RQ3 also relabels the CBSA-specific gaps as "between-CBSA variation" (p.10). That phrase collides with Table 1's "Within division between CBSA" component, and a reader could conflate the two.

The claim that within-CBSA inequality is "by far the largest source" (p.10) holds for Black–White gaps: 0.944 + 0.258 = 1.202 vs 0.303 between CBSAs (Table 1, 2018). It is much weaker for Hispanic–White gaps: 0.491 + 0.105 = 0.596 vs 0.476.

*Abstract fidelity.* The abstract accurately states the data, the SSG/LEO distinction, and the direction of the gaps. It has four problems:

- It overstates universality ("across all geographic scales and for LEOs"), as discussed above.
- Its "arises from" and "structural" language suggests causation that a descriptive, residual-closed decomposition cannot deliver.
- It omits the paper's third RQ and its segregation finding entirely.
- It omits the offsetting negative between-region residual and the fact that the Black–White combined gap did not change significantly.

*Tables and figures.*

- **Table 1** is legible and honestly annotated. Its column labels "2018/2021" differ from the text's "2017–2018/2020–2021," which is minor.
- **Figure 1** has the definitional contradiction and weighting issues noted above. It covers 2017–2018 only (note, p.9).
- **Figure 2** has six panels with linear and quadratic weighted fits. Several details are missing or inconsistent:
  - The y-axis reads "Difference in Exposure to Security," not SSGs specifically, and gives no units (presumably per 1,000 students).
  - Tick labels are very small in print.
  - Marker size varies but is not explained; the note mentions weighting only for the fit lines.
  - The number of CBSAs is not given.
  
  A reader cannot tell from the exhibit whether the outcome is SSG-only, as the title says.

*Density.* The paper is short enough that little can be skipped. The load-bearing material is Table 1, the RQ2 paragraphs on p.8, and the RQ3 paragraph on p.10. The introduction's policy history (pp.1–3) is background.

*Other internal-consistency notes:*

- The missing-data text says "around 3% of total observations were missing … in our two focal waves," attributed mainly to NYCPS in 2017–2018. It then says "approximately 5% of schools were missing data" in 2020–2021 (pp.4–5). Readers cannot reconcile the two figures or learn how missing schools were treated.
- The data section says the CCD supplies "free lunch program eligibility" (p.5), while footnote 3 (p.12) measures poverty exposure with free or reduced-price lunch.
- The CRDC staffing comparison, "30,000 FTE SSGs compared to 22,000 FTE SROs" (p.4), labels the second group SROs rather than LEOs and gives no year or source.
- Footnotes 1–3 all resolve (p.12). Footnote 2's Theil index range (0–1) is consistent with the Figure 2 axes (0–0.5).

**Text-vs-table check:**

- B–W combined gap 2018 "1.16" (text, p.6) vs 1.163 (Table 1, p.7): MATCH
- B–W combined gap 2021 "1.02," change p = .110, level p < .001 (p.6) vs 1.021 (0.110; 0.000): MATCH
- H–W combined gap "0.79" to "0.66," change p = .04, level p < .001 (p.6) vs 0.792; 0.656 (0.040; 0.000): MATCH
- B–W SSG "0.97," LEO "0.17" (p.6) vs 0.974, 0.172: MATCH (but 0.97 + 0.17 ≠ 1.16; subtype non-additivity unexplained: MISMATCH in the implied partition)
- "0.87 times the mean" (p.6): 0.974/1.11 = 0.88, MATCH given the prose inputs; the mean 1.11 and SD 2.15 appear only in prose, not in any table: NOT REPORTED in an exhibit (population and year of these moments unstated)
- "0.45 SD" (p.6): 0.974/2.15 = 0.453, MATCH
- LEO "0.26 SD" (p.6): implies an LEO SD of about 0.66 (0.172/0.26); the LEO mean and SD are not given anywhere: NOT REPORTED
- H–W SSG gaps "0.75" and "0.71" (p.6) vs 0.749, 0.712: MATCH
- H–W LEO "no different from zero in 2018" (p.8) vs 0.026 (0.158): MATCH
- H–W LEO "slightly negative in 2021 (p = .001)" (p.8) vs −0.055 (0.001; 0.000): MISMATCH (.001 is the change-test p-value)
- Between-district B–W "0.94" and "0.83" (p.8) vs 0.944, 0.832: MATCH
- "roughly 80% of the total gap" (p.8): 0.944/1.163 = 81%, 0.832/1.021 = 81%, MATCH against the net gap; ill-defined as a share because the residual is negative (positive components sum to 1.519 in 2018)
- Between-CBSA B–W "0.30" and "0.26" (p.8) vs 0.303, 0.262: MATCH (2021 value has p = .090 vs zero, not flagged in text)
- Between-school B–W "0.26" and "0.24" (p.8) vs 0.258, 0.243: MATCH
- H–W between-CBSA and between-district 2018 "0.48 and 0.49," between-school "0.105" (p.8) vs 0.476, 0.491, 0.105: MATCH
- H–W 2021 "0.442" and "0.372," change p = .247, level p < .001 (p.8) vs 0.442, 0.372 (0.247; 0.000): MATCH
- Between-region "−0.356 and −0.295" (p.8) vs −0.356, −0.295: MATCH
- Residual closure (Table 1, p.7): B–W 2018 combined 0.014 + 0.303 + 0.944 + 0.258 − 0.356 = 1.163; SSG 0.034 + 0.294 + 0.826 + 0.183 − 0.363 = 0.974; B–W 2021 combined 0.033 + 0.262 + 0.832 + 0.243 − 0.349 = 1.021; SSG 0.041 + 0.256 + 0.738 + 0.146 − 0.358 = 0.823; H–W 2018 combined 0.015 + 0.476 + 0.491 + 0.105 − 0.295 = 0.792; H–W 2021 combined 0.024 + 0.442 + 0.372 + 0.083 − 0.265 = 0.656: MATCH. Closure is guaranteed by construction because the row is defined as the residual.
- Significant 2018-to-2021 changes (first 2021 p < .05, Table 1): B–W SSG (0.035), NOT MENTIONED; H–W combined (0.040), MENTIONED; H–W LEO (0.001), MENTIONED only as a level: MISMATCH. No component-level change is significant; the prose correctly treats the one it discusses (H–W between-district, p = .247) as non-significant.
- "gaps remain at every other finer spatial level—division, CBSA, and district" (p.8) vs division components 0.014 (p = .934) and 0.015 (p = .910): MISMATCH
- Abstract "present across all geographic scales and for LEOs" (p.1) vs non-significant division components and non-positive H–W LEO gaps: MISMATCH
- "Equation (1)" in the Table 1 note: does not resolve in the main text; "Supplemental Appendix Equation 1": not available
- Tables A1–A3, Figure A1 (pp.6, 8, 10): cited consistently; contents not available
- Footnotes 1–3: resolve (p.12)
- RQ3 multivariate regression (p.10): NOT REPORTED in any main-text exhibit
- Figure 2 (p.11): bivariate only, with weighted linear and quadratic fits; CBSA N not reported; y-axis units unstated and labeled "Security" rather than SSG: NOT REPORTED (N, units)
- Racial composition "proportion of non-White students" (p.6) vs Figure 2 "Black/Hispanic Enrollment Share": MISMATCH
- Figure 1 x-axis: title and axis say within-region percent; note formula Black_r/ΣBlack_r and text (p.8) say share of the national population; plotted values sum to about 0.56 (Panel A): MISMATCH
- Figure 1 "clear downward slope" (p.8): N = 4, LEO line slopes upward in Panel A, fit weighted by the x-variable: MISMATCH (overstated)
- High-school analytic sample size (schools, districts, CBSAs): NOT REPORTED (only the all-school count of about 80,000 schools and about 13,000 districts, p.5)

---

### Contribution Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)  
**Internal confidence estimate:** 0.76

This brief adds one useful descriptive fact to the school-policing literature. Using universe CRDC data for U.S. public high schools, it shows that Black–White (and Hispanic–White) gaps in security staffing per 1,000 students come mostly from non-sworn school security guards (SSGs), not from sworn law enforcement officers (LEOs). For Black students, the gap arises mainly between districts within the same metro area. That is new, credible at the descriptive level, and directly relevant to the police-free-schools debate. The paper is weaker beyond that core. The regional "paradox," the claim that segregation is the "only significant predictor" (RQ3), and the talk of districts substituting SSGs for LEOs all go further than the evidence shown in the main text. The first rests on four data points and an unestimated residual. The second is close to mechanical and its regression is not reported in the main text. The third is untested.

**Strengths:**

- **[CHECKABLE]** The paper looks past sworn officers to guards and does so with national universe data. It uses two CRDC waves (2017–18, 2020–21) covering about 80,000 schools per year from nearly 13,000 districts (text, pp.4–5). Its stated gap in the literature is that prior studies of racial inequality in school-policing exposure "have focused exclusively on LEOs" (text, p.3).
- **[CHECKABLE]** The headline fact is simple and big enough to matter. In 2017–18 the overall Black–White high-school gap was 1.163 personnel per 1,000 students, and 0.974 of it came from SSGs versus 0.172 from LEOs (Table 1, p.7; text, p.6). The SSG gap is about 0.87 times mean SSG exposure (1.11 per 1,000, SD = 2.15) and about 0.45 SD (text, p.6). The Hispanic–White gap is essentially all SSGs: 0.749 SSG versus 0.026 LEO (p = .158) in 2018 (Table 1, p.7).
- **[CHECKABLE]** The geographic decomposition locates the Black–White disparity. The between-district, within-CBSA component is 0.944 in 2018 and 0.832 in 2021, about 80% of the national gap in each year (Table 1, p.7; text, p.8). The within-district, between-school components are much smaller (0.258 and 0.243; Table 1, p.7).
- **[JUDGMENT]** The exposure framing (staffing intensity per 1,000 students, not just whether any officer is present) is a real improvement over prevalence-only descriptions in this literature. The paper explains why the distinction matters for large secondary schools (text, pp.3–5).
- **[CHECKABLE]** The Black–White versus Hispanic–White contrast is informative. The Hispanic–White gap is split more evenly between the between-CBSA component (0.476) and the between-district component (0.491) in 2018 (Table 1, p.7; text, p.8), which suggests different geographic mechanisms for the two groups.
- **[JUDGMENT]** The paper stays honest about the limits of causal claims in its framing. It presents itself as "the descriptive component of the school security personnel story" (text, p.3) and says there is no rigorous causal evidence on the effects of SSGs (text, p.2). That is the right scope for a Brief.

**Weaknesses:**

- **[CHECKABLE]** The RQ3 headline is reported but not shown. The paper says that in "multivariate regression results," racial segregation is "the strongest and only significant predictor" (text, p.10). Figure 2 (p.11) shows only bivariate scatterplots with linear and quadratic fits. The main text gives no coefficients, standard errors, or number of CBSAs, and it does not say where the multivariate table is. The LEO counterpart (Supplemental Figure A1) is not available.
- **[JUDGMENT]** The segregation finding is close to built in. A within-CBSA exposure gap cannot exist without between-school or between-district racial separation, and the authors themselves call segregation "a necessary but not sufficient component" (text, p.6). So segregation predicting the gap is largely expected by construction. The reading that SSG disparities are "fundamentally associated with structural segregation rather than school demographics or resource differences," and that deployment "operate[s] independently of racial composition or poverty concentration" (text, p.10), goes beyond what a CBSA-level cross-sectional association can show.
- **[CHECKABLE]** The regional "paradox" rests on thin evidence. The between-region component (−0.356 Black–White, −0.295 Hispanic–White, 2018) is a residual that "is not estimated" (Table 1 note, p.7). Figure 1 (p.9) fits lines through N = 4 regions. In Panel A (Black), the LEO fit line slopes upward, not downward (Figure 1, p.9). So the text's claim that "regions with larger minority shares staff fewer security personnel" (text, p.8) holds for SSGs and for the combined measure, not for LEOs.
- **[CHECKABLE]** The Panel A x-axis values in Figure 1 run from about .05 to .23 across the four regions (Figure 1, p.9). They cannot sum to 1, so they look like within-region Black enrollment shares. Yet the note formula (Black_r/ΣBlack_r) and the text ("share of the national Black ... student population," p.8) describe each region's share of national Black enrollment. Readers cannot tell which quantity is plotted.
- **[CHECKABLE]** The substitution story is untested, and the paper's own two waves cut the other way. The Discussion suggests districts "may be reallocating SSGs as substitutes for LEOs" (text, p.10). But the Black–White SSG gap *fell* from 0.974 to 0.823 between 2018 and 2021 (p = .035 for the change), while the LEO gap stayed flat at 0.172 versus 0.179 (p = .863) (Table 1, p.7). The text does not discuss the significant SSG decline.
- **[CHECKABLE]** The main text never mentions COVID-19 or the pandemic, although one of the two waves is 2020–21 (text, pp.4–8). That year's staffing counts and the 2018–2021 changes are therefore hard to interpret as trends.
- **[CHECKABLE]** Missing data sit in a consequential place. About 3% of observations lack security-personnel data, "most notably" New York City Public Schools in 2017–18, and about 5% of schools are missing it in 2020–21 (text, p.4). The main text does not say how the affected schools were handled (dropped, imputed, or otherwise). **[JUDGMENT]** NYC is the largest district in a large CBSA, and between-district-within-CBSA variation is the paper's main finding, so this matters for both the 2018 levels and the change between years.
- **[CHECKABLE]** Several framing numbers lack context. "30,000 FTE SSGs compared to 22,000 FTE SROs" (text, p.4) is given without a year or source. The size of the high-school analytic sample is not reported in the main text. Robustness to all-school and state-level decompositions is asserted but lives in Supplemental Tables A1–A3 (text, pp.6, 8), which are not available. Neither is Equation 1, which underlies Table 1.
- **[JUDGMENT]** The combined "school security personnel" measure counts one SSG FTE the same as one LEO FTE. The finding that "the disparity mainly arises from differences in exposure to SSGs" (abstract, p.1) is therefore a statement about headcount, not about harm, arrest exposure, or disciplinary consequences, where LEOs' arrest authority may matter far more per FTE.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- *Cite it for:* the national descriptive fact that in U.S. public high schools in 2017–18 and 2020–21, Black students had more security staff per 1,000 students than White students (1.163 and 1.021; Table 1, p.7), and that most of this gap is SSGs, not sworn officers (0.974 of 1.163 in 2018; Table 1, p.7).
- *Cite it for:* the Hispanic–White security-staffing gap coming almost entirely from SSGs, with no meaningful Hispanic–White LEO gap (0.026, p = .158, in 2018; Table 1, p.7).
- *Cite it for:* the Black–White staffing gap being concentrated between districts within the same metro area (about 80% of the national gap; Table 1, p.7; text, p.8), not between schools within districts. This is a useful signal that district-level allocation and between-district segregation are where to look.
- *Cite it, carefully, for:* the policy-relevant point that removing sworn officers alone (as in the Chicago example, text, p.2) would leave most of the measured staffing disparity in place. This follows arithmetically from the SSG/LEO split. It says nothing about outcomes.
- *Do not cite it for:* evidence that segregation *causes* SSG disparities, or that SSG deployment is "independent" of poverty or racial composition. The relationship is partly mechanical, the evidence is cross-sectional and bivariate in the displayed figure, and the multivariate estimates are not shown in the main text.
- *Do not cite it for:* evidence that districts are substituting guards for police. This is conjecture, and the paper's own data show the Black–White SSG gap narrowing from 2018 to 2021 (Table 1, p.7).
- *Do not cite it for:* the regional "paradox" (regions with more students of color use less security staff) as an established pattern. It rests on four points and an unestimated residual, and it does not hold for LEOs in the Black panel (Figure 1, p.9; Table 1 note, p.7).
- *Do not cite it for:* a 2018–2021 trend, or for effects of the police-free-schools movement. There are two waves, one of them a pandemic year the paper does not discuss.
- *Do not cite it for:* claims that students of color are more "surveilled" (text, p.10) in any sense beyond staffing ratios. The paper does not measure what guards do, how much contact they have with students, or what happens to students as a result.
- *Open questions:* What do SSGs do, and do they affect discipline, arrests, or sense of belonging? Are the within-CBSA district gaps driven by a few large urban districts or spread widely? How much of the gap remains after conditioning on school size, urbanicity, and incident rates? How did NYC's missing data affect the estimates? Do later CRDC waves show the gaps shrinking, holding steady, or shifting toward SSGs?

**Detailed Commentary:**

*What is new.* **[JUDGMENT]** The core novelty is empirical and substantive, not methodological. Earlier CRDC-based descriptions of racial patterning in school policing (the paper cites Lindsay et al., 2018 and Gleit, 2022; text, pp.3–4) focus on sworn officers. This brief adds guards, measures exposure by staffing intensity, and decomposes the national gap by geographic level. The decomposition follows Goldhaber et al. (2015) (text, p.5), so the method is a transfer to a new domain, not an innovation. For a Brief that is fine: a well-documented, policy-relevant descriptive fact is exactly what the genre is for. The question matters. SSGs outnumber LEOs by the paper's count (text, p.4), and a policy debate focused on removing sworn officers could miss most of the staffing disparity. Whether SSGs harm or help students is a separate, open question that the paper correctly defers to future work.

*How strong the core fact is.* **[CHECKABLE]** The 2018 Black–White SSG gap (0.974; Table 1, p.7) is large relative to the SSG distribution: 0.87 times the mean and 0.45 SD (text, p.6). The LEO gap is 0.172, about 0.26 SD (text, p.6). **[JUDGMENT]** These are unadjusted, student-weighted descriptive gaps, and that is the right primary estimand for a question about who is exposed. Readers should still remember that the paper does not show how much of the gap reflects school size, urbanicity, building characteristics, or incident rates. Those are exactly the factors the paper says guide placement (text, p.3). The SSG-dominant pattern is the most robust and most quotable finding, and it deserves to become the standard reference for "guards, not just police." Its reach is a claim about staffing counts, and the combined measure weights guards and sworn officers equally.

*The geographic decomposition.* **[CHECKABLE]** For Black–White gaps, the four estimated components sum to more than the national total (0.014 + 0.303 + 0.944 + 0.258 = 1.519 against 1.163 in 2018; Table 1, p.7). The difference, −0.356, is assigned to a between-region residual that "is not estimated" (Table 1 note, p.7). **[JUDGMENT]** So the "roughly 80%" figure for the between-district component (text, p.8) is a share of a total that includes a large negative offset. Measured against the sum of the positive components, the between-district share is closer to three-fifths. The qualitative conclusion that between-district, within-metro variation is the largest single source for Black–White gaps survives either way. The percentage should be quoted with that caveat. The claim on p.10 that within-CBSA inequality is "by far the largest source" fits the Black–White gap. It fits the Hispanic–White gap much less well: the between-CBSA component (0.476) is close to the between-district component (0.491) (Table 1, p.7). The paper's own RQ2 text acknowledges this (p.8), but the RQ3 motivation on p.10 does not.

*The regional "paradox."* **[JUDGMENT]** The observation on p.10 is interesting and worth following up: regions enrolling more Black and Hispanic students staff fewer security personnel on average, while within those regions students of color are more exposed. As evidence, though, it has three problems. It is a residual with no standard error (Table 1 note, p.7). It is illustrated with four points (Figure 1, p.9). And it is tied to funding differences (Lee et al., 2022) that the paper does not test (text, p.8). **[CHECKABLE]** Figure 1 Panel A also shows the LEO line rising with the regional Black share (Figure 1, p.9), which matches the small positive LEO between-region residual (0.009; Table 1, p.7). So the pattern is specific to SSGs. Readers should treat this as a hypothesis the brief raises, not a result.

*RQ3 and the mechanism language.* **[JUDGMENT]** RQ3 is where the paper's interpretation most outruns its evidence. A CBSA's Black–White exposure gap is, by construction, zero when schools are racially identical. Racial separation is the channel through which any staffing difference becomes a racial exposure gap, which is why the authors call segregation necessary (text, p.6). Finding that segregation "predicts" the gap therefore confirms that the gap needs segregation to exist. It does not show that "SSG deployment patterns operate independently of racial composition or poverty concentration" (text, p.10). The null results for composition and poverty also come from a multivariate model the main text does not report and in which the predictors are likely correlated with each other. The LEO null (Supplemental Figure A1, not available) is described as evidence that "LEO placement follows entirely different mechanisms" (text, p.10). Failing to predict a small gap (0.172; Table 1, p.7) with three variables does not show that a different mechanism exists. The Figure 2 scatterplots (p.11) are useful descriptively, since they show wide variation across metros in SSG gaps. The causal-sounding summary points (a)–(c) on p.10 are the paper's most quotable lines and its least well supported.

*Time comparison and policy framing.* **[CHECKABLE]** The Black–White SSG gap narrowed significantly between waves (0.974 to 0.823, p = .035), while the LEO gap did not change (p = .863) (Table 1, p.7). The Hispanic–White overall gap also narrowed (0.792 to 0.656, p = .040; Table 1, p.7; text, p.6). **[JUDGMENT]** Because the text does not mention the pandemic and 2020–21 was an unusual year, these changes are hard to read either way. They do not, however, fit the Discussion's suggestion that guards are replacing police in ways that preserve surveillance of students of color (text, p.10). The Chicago policy implication, that removing LEOs alone leaves the SSG disparity in place, follows from the cross-sectional split and is the paper's most defensible policy point. The broader recommendations about funding formulas and staffing discretion (text, p.12) are reasonable directions for inquiry, not conclusions from this analysis.

*Generalizability and boundaries.* **[JUDGMENT]** The results should generalize well across U.S. public high schools, because the data cover the universe of schools and the authors report consistent patterns in all-school and state-level versions (text, p.8; Tables A1–A3 not available). The boundaries are time, measurement, and meaning. There are two waves, one pandemic-affected. The CRDC's staffing counts are school-reported, with known quality problems in some districts (text, p.4), including missing NYC data whose handling is not described. And FTE counts do not capture roles, contact, or consequences. The paper states its descriptive purpose clearly (text, p.3), but its Discussion and RQ3 summary do not keep to that scope as consistently as the framing does.

*Standing in the literature.* **[JUDGMENT]** Among the work the paper cites, this looks like the most direct national evidence on racial disparities in exposure to school security guards specifically, and on the geographic scale of disparities in exposure to security staff overall. It should become the reference for those descriptive facts. It sets up several follow-on studies: causal evaluations of SSGs (the paper cites Vernon & Curran, 2024 as related correlational work; text, p.2); district-level analyses of how security budgets are allocated across schools; analyses conditioning on school size, urbanicity, and incident rates to separate composition from allocation; and later-wave updates that can speak to whether the post-2020 police-free-schools reforms shifted staffing toward guards. Whether later CRDC waves now exist that would allow a cleaner post-2020 comparison is something readers should check. The paper describes its two waves as "the two most recent" (text, p.4).

---

### Reproducibility Review

**Rating:** Weak (moderate confidence)  
**Internal confidence estimate:** 0.70

All three data sources (CRDC, CCD, SEDA) are public, so this study could in principle be rebuilt by anyone. But the article gives no data availability statement, no code, no software, no analytic sample size for the high-school sample, and no standard-error method. The estimating equation and "technical details" are deferred to an online supplement that was not available for this review. Table 1's decomposition is internally consistent: every residual "between region" entry checks against the other rows. Even so, a replicator would have to guess at several consequential construction steps, and the RQ3 multivariate regression behind the paper's headline "segregation is the only significant predictor" claim is not reported anywhere in the article.

**Strengths:**

- **[CHECKABLE]** All inputs are public, federally produced files: CRDC 2017–18 and 2020–21 (text, p.4), CCD enrollment by race/ethnicity and free-lunch eligibility (text, p.5), and SEDA for CBSA identifiers and segregation indices (text, p.5; note 2, p.12). No restricted-use data or data-use agreement stands between a reader and the raw inputs.
- **[CHECKABLE]** The paper explains why the 2015–16 CRDC wave was excluded ("reporting issues that affected data from more than 69,000 schools," text, p.4). It also flags the New York City 2017–18 "force-certified" security-staffing problem by name, and gives approximate missingness rates for security-staffing items: about 3% overall and about 5% in 2020–21 (text, p.4).
- **[CHECKABLE]** The weighting principle of the decomposition is stated in words: school-level components are weighted by the number of Black (or Hispanic) and White students enrolled (text, p.5). The estimand is stated as the average difference in school-level staffing per 1,000 students experienced by the two groups (text, p.5).
- **[CHECKABLE]** Table 1 is arithmetically transparent. The note says the between-region row is "the residual of the overall gap minus the sum of the gaps at each geographic scale" (Table 1 note, p.7). All 12 residual cells reproduce from the printed entries. For example, Black–White 2018 total: 1.163 − (0.014 + 0.303 + 0.944 + 0.258) = −0.356; Hispanic–White 2021 SSG: 0.712 − (0.039 + 0.435 + 0.354 + 0.057) = −0.173 (Table 1, p.7).
- **[CHECKABLE]** The prose matches Table 1 on the headline numbers: the 1.16 and 1.02 Black–White gaps and the p = .110 test for change (text p.6 vs. Table 1, p.7), the 0.79 and 0.66 Hispanic–White gaps and p = .04 (text p.6; Table 1 shows 0.040), and "roughly 80%" from the between-district component (0.944/1.163 ≈ 0.81 and 0.832/1.021 ≈ 0.81; text p.8, Table 1 p.7). The standardized SSG gap is also internally consistent: 0.974/2.15 ≈ 0.45 SD and 0.974/1.11 ≈ 0.88 times the mean (text, p.6).
- **[CHECKABLE]** Robustness to alternative samples and geographic units (all schools; states in place of CBSAs) is reported to exist in Supplemental Tables A1–A3 (text, p.8). These are not available for this review.

**Weaknesses:**

- **[CHECKABLE]** The article has no data availability statement, no replication-package or repository link, and no "code available on request" line. The only pointer is "Supplemental material for this article is available online" (p.12). **[JUDGMENT]** With entirely public data, the usual reason for not posting code does not apply, so this falls short of journal-era norms.
- **[CHECKABLE]** No statistical software or package is named anywhere in the article.
- **[CHECKABLE]** The analytic sample for the headline (high-school) analysis is never given: no count of high schools, districts, or CBSAs. The only N is for all schools, "about 80,000 schools each year from nearly 13,000 school districts" (text, p.5). Table 1 reports no N (p.7), Figure 2 does not report how many CBSAs are plotted (p.11), and Figure 1 gives only N = 4 regions (p.9).
- **[CHECKABLE]** "High school" is not defined: no grade span, CCD school-level code, or CRDC flag. The paper says only that it focuses on high schools because security personnel are more common there (text, p.6).
- **[CHECKABLE]** The linking key between CRDC, CCD, and SEDA is not stated. The paper says SEDA was used "to obtain identifier information on CBSAs" (text, p.5) but does not say whether CBSA is assigned at the school, district, or county level. It also does not say how schools outside any CBSA are handled. By the paper's own figure, CBSAs cover 95% of the U.S. population (text, p.6), so some schools must fall outside one.
- **[CHECKABLE]** The nesting of CBSAs within Census divisions is asserted ("between CBSAs within the same Census division," text, p.5), yet the paper notes that CBSAs "can encompass multiple state boundaries" (text, p.6). How cross-division CBSAs are assigned is not stated. **[JUDGMENT]** I believe several large CBSAs (e.g., Philadelphia, St. Louis, Cincinnati, Memphis) span two Census divisions. If so, their assignment affects the "within division between CBSA" and "within CBSA between district" rows, and those rows carry the paper's main RQ2 finding.
- **[CHECKABLE]** The winsorization rule is underspecified. The text says about 200 observations had "extreme FTE values" and that values "that exceeded three times the 99th percentile" were winsorized (text, p.5; note 1, p.12). It does not say (a) what value they were replaced with (3 × p99? p99?); (b) whether the percentile was computed by year, school level, and personnel type, or pooled; (c) whether the rule was applied separately to SSG, LEO, and combined rates; or (d) how many observations the rule actually changed, as opposed to the ~200 "identified."
- **[CHECKABLE]** SSG and LEO gaps do not add up to the combined "school security personnel" gap in Table 1. Examples: Black–White 2018, 0.974 + 0.172 = 1.146 vs. 1.163; Black–White 2021, 0.823 + 0.179 = 1.002 vs. 1.021; Hispanic–White 2018, 0.749 + 0.026 = 0.775 vs. 0.792 (Table 1, p.7). The text shows the same gap ("1.16 … Of this total, 0.97 … were SSGs and 0.17 were LEOs," text p.6) without explaining it. **[JUDGMENT]** The likeliest causes are winsorizing each measure separately or using different samples because of item-level missingness. Neither is documented, and a replicator matching these numbers would have to guess which.
- **[CHECKABLE]** The paper does not say what was done with missing security-staffing data: listwise deletion, imputation, or zero-filling. The same goes for the NYC 2017–18 force-certified records, which the paper describes (text, p.4) without stating whether NYC was dropped for 2017–18. CRDC reserve/suppression codes are also not addressed.
- **[CHECKABLE]** Neither the estimating equation nor the decomposition formula appears in the main text. Table 1 cites "Equation (1)" and "Supplemental Appendix Equation 1" (Table 1 note, p.7), and the text defers "technical details" to the supplement (text, p.6). Not available for this review.
- **[CHECKABLE]** Table 1 reports point estimates with p-values only: no standard errors, no confidence intervals (p.7). The article never says how the p-values were obtained (analytic, bootstrap, clustered at district or CBSA, or treating schools as independent), and the word "cluster" appears only in a substantive sense ("clusters of states," p.8). The 2018-vs-2021 change tests come from a pooled regression in the supplement (Table 1 note, p.7). How the repeat observation of the same schools across waves was handled is not stated.
- **[CHECKABLE]** The between-region row is a residual and "is not estimated" (Table 1 note, p.7), so it has no p-value. Yet it is the basis for a substantive interpretive claim about regional funding regimes (text, pp.8–10).
- **[CHECKABLE]** The RQ3 multivariate regression is described only in words: "racial segregation is the strongest and only significant predictor" (text, p.10). The main text gives no coefficients, standard errors, N of CBSAs, weights, year, or model specification, and it gives no pointer to a supplemental table for these results. The supplemental pointer on p.10 refers only to Figure A1, for LEOs.
- **[CHECKABLE]** The note for Figure 2 does not state the survey year, the number of CBSAs, any minimum-size or minimum-enrollment rule for including a CBSA, or what marker size represents. It says fits are "weighted by the Black or Hispanic student share" without saying share of what (p.11). The figure is an embedded raster image, and its axis tick labels are legible only under heavy zoom (p.11).
- **[CHECKABLE]** Figure 1's x-variable is described inconsistently. The text calls it each region's "share of the national Black (Panel A) or Hispanic (Panel B) student population" (text, p.8), and the note's example formula (Black_r / ΣBlack_r) reads the same way. But the axis is labeled "Percent of High School Students in Census Region: Black/Hispanic" (Figure 1, p.9). The four Panel A x-values, which I read approximately from the plot as ~0.05 to ~0.23, sum to well under 1, so they cannot be shares of a national total (Figure 1, p.9). The note's weighting is also unusual: the fit is weighted by the x-variable itself (Figure 1 note, p.9).
- **[CHECKABLE]** It is not stated whether the mean SSG exposure of 1.11 per 1,000 (SD = 2.15) (text, p.6) is a school-level or student-weighted statistic, or which year and sample it uses. **[JUDGMENT]** Figure 1's regional SSG means all fall at or below roughly 1.3, with the South near 0.35 (approximate readings, Figure 1, p.9). A student-weighted national mean of 1.11 looks hard to square with those values, which suggests the 1.11 and 2.15 are on a different basis. The "0.45 SD" and "0.87 times the mean" scalings (text, p.6) therefore cannot be interpreted with confidence.
- **[CHECKABLE]** Poverty-exposure inputs are described inconsistently: "free lunch program eligibility" from CCD (text, p.5) vs. "free or reduced-price lunch (FRPL)" (note 3, p.12). The SEDA version and file used for segregation indices and CBSA identifiers are not named (text, p.5; note 2, p.12).
- **[CHECKABLE]** Minor: the text says Hispanic–White LEO gaps were "slightly negative in 2021 (p = .001)" (text, p.8). In Table 1, 0.001 is the p-value for the change from 2018; the p-value against zero is 0.000 (Table 1, p.7). The FTE totals on p.4 ("30,000 FTE SSGs compared to 22,000 FTE SROs") give no year or source.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- **Get the supplement first.** Before relying on Table 1's significance tests or the year-over-year comparisons, read Supplemental Appendix Equation 1 and the technical details (not available for this review). Check that they specify (i) the regression form of the decomposition, including which fixed effects define each geographic level; (ii) the standard-error method and any clustering; and (iii) the analytic N of high schools, districts, and CBSAs by year. If the supplement lacks these, the p-values in Table 1 cannot be checked independently.
- **Rebuilding the data.** A replicator needs the CRDC school-level security-staffing FTE items for both waves. I believe these are the school-support variables for sworn law-enforcement officer FTE and security-guard FTE (in the 2017–18 public file, I believe named SCH_FTESECURITY_LEO and SCH_FTESECURITY_GUA). They also need CCD school-level membership by race/ethnicity and the free/FRPL counts, plus the SEDA crosswalk that carries CBSA (and, for RQ3, SEDA's Theil-index segregation measures). The paper names none of these files or variables, so a replicator should confirm the item names against CRDC documentation and ask the authors which merge key and SEDA release they used.
- **Decisions to pin down with the authors, not guess:** the high-school definition; the winsorization cap value and the grouping used for the 99th percentile; whether NYC 2017–18 and other missing or reserve-coded records were dropped; how non-CBSA schools and cross-division CBSAs were handled; and why SSG + LEO ≠ total in Table 1.
- **Most reproducible result.** The national Black–White and Hispanic–White exposure gaps (Table 1, "Overall gap (USA)," p.7) are a weighted difference in means on public data and should be approximately reproducible even without code. Treat an independent recomputation landing near 1.16 (Black–White, 2018) and 0.79 (Hispanic–White, 2018) as a reasonable first check (Table 1, p.7).
- **The RQ2 geographic shares** (e.g., the ~80% between-district share, text p.8) depend on nesting and CBSA-assignment choices that are undocumented. Replicators should expect sensitivity here and test alternative assignments.
- **Treat the RQ3 claim as effectively unverifiable as reported.** The claim that segregation is "the strongest and only significant predictor" (text, p.10), and the three interpretive conclusions (a)–(c) drawn from it (text, p.10), rest on a regression whose coefficients, standard errors, N, weights, and specification are not shown in the article. Figure 2 shows bivariate associations only (p.11). Ask the authors for the regression table before citing this result.
- **Figure 1** should not be used to read off regional "shares of the national minority population." Given the inconsistency between the text (p.8) and the axis (p.9), the x-axis appears to show within-region percentages. The regression lines rest on four points (N = 4 regions, p.9).

**Detailed Commentary:**

This is a descriptive brief built entirely on public federal data, which is the best case for reproducibility. No restricted-use license or data-use agreement blocks a would-be replicator, and the whole pipeline (CRDC staffing counts, CCD enrollments, SEDA geography and segregation indices) could be posted as a small script. Measured against that opportunity, the article's transparency is thin. It has no data or code availability statement, no repository, no named software, and none of the sample-size reporting a reader would expect for a table whose rows are all significance tests. Because the paper is a Brief, some methodological detail can reasonably live in a supplement, and the authors say that the estimating equation and technical details are there (Table 1 note, p.7; text, p.6). I could not see that supplement. So my rating reflects the article as a self-contained record, and it could move toward the lower end of "Adequate" if the supplement supplies the equation, Ns, and the standard-error method. It could not move further on the article alone, because the gaps listed below are construction decisions, not estimator algebra. A supplement containing only Equation 1 would not close them.

The strongest part of the reporting is Table 1's internal logic. Every between-region residual reproduces exactly from the other rows (Table 1, p.7), and the text's headline figures match the table. A reader can at least confirm that the numbers in the table say what the prose says they say. A careful reader also notices two things the article does not explain. First, SSG and LEO gaps do not sum to the combined-personnel gap. The difference is about 0.017 per 1,000 for the Black–White 2018 total, and it recurs in sub-rows, such as within-CBSA 0.826 + 0.103 = 0.929 vs. 0.944 (Table 1, p.7). The discrepancies are small substantively, but they show that the three outcome columns were not built from one common sample with one common transformation. The paper's documentation does not let a reader determine which step differs. The winsorization rule is the most likely source. The rule is described as capping values above "three times the 99th percentile" (text, p.5), but it gives no replacement value, grouping, or count of observations actually changed. Winsorizing SSG, LEO, and total rates separately would produce exactly this pattern of non-additivity.

The second gap is the analytic sample. The only N in the paper is for all schools, about 80,000 per year (text, p.5), while every headline result is for high schools, which are never defined or counted. Missing security-staffing data is described in some detail, including the NYC 2017–18 force-certification problem and approximate missingness of 3% and 5% (text, p.4). The paper does not say what was done about it. This matters for more than bookkeeping. **[JUDGMENT]** New York City enrolls a very large number of Black and Hispanic high-school students. If NYC was dropped in 2017–18 but retained in 2020–21, the between-year change tests in Table 1 (e.g., p = .110 for the Black–White total, p = .035 for Black–White SSGs; Table 1, p.7) would partly reflect a composition change. The article does not let a reader rule this out.

The geographic decomposition raises its own replication questions. The nesting runs school within district within CBSA within division within region (text, p.5). The paper describes CBSAs as able to cross state lines (text, p.6) but does not explain how CBSAs that cross Census-division boundaries, or schools outside any CBSA, are placed in that hierarchy. Because the paper's central RQ2 message is that "roughly 80%" of the Black–White gap arises between districts within CBSAs (text, p.8), these assignment rules are not peripheral. The between-region row is a residual with no uncertainty attached (Table 1 note, p.7), yet it supports a fairly specific interpretive claim about regional funding regimes (text, pp.8–10). Figure 1, offered as illustration of that residual, has an x-axis that the text (p.8) and the axis label (p.9) describe differently. The plotted values are consistent only with the axis-label reading.

RQ3 is the least verifiable part of the paper. The article reports that multivariate regressions show segregation to be "the strongest and only significant predictor" of between-CBSA variation in SSG exposure gaps (text, p.10), and it draws three conclusions from that result (text, p.10). The main text contains no coefficient, standard error, sample size, weight definition, year, or model statement for these regressions, and it does not point to where they appear. Figure 2 shows only bivariate scatterplots with linear and quadratic fits (p.11). Its note omits the year, the number of CBSAs, any inclusion threshold (CBSA-specific gaps for small CBSAs will be extremely noisy), and what "Black or Hispanic student share" means as a weight. The figure is a low-resolution raster whose tick labels are barely readable (p.11). A reader cannot regenerate Figure 2 from the description, and cannot check the RQ3 inference at all.

On balance, the national gap estimates in the first row of Table 1 are probably approximately reproducible by a competent analyst with the public files, because they are enrollment-weighted differences in school-level staffing rates and the weighting is described (text, p.5). The geographic shares are reproducible only up to several undocumented assignment and sample decisions. The between-year significance tests depend on an equation and standard-error method that are not available from the article. The RQ3 multivariate finding must currently be taken on trust. For a study whose inputs are all public, posting a short replication script and a data availability statement would have resolved almost every issue above. Readers should ask the authors for that material before building on the RQ2 decomposition shares or the RQ3 segregation result.
